title: Is this what I feared?
hook: Seneca: set aside days to live on very little and ask if this is what you dreaded (Letters 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday: plain food, Musonius's training at the table. Your line was plain is training.

Day three hundred. Worth a breath of its own. Now a quieter question, one that can sit in the back of a mind for years: what if it all went away? The job, the savings, the comfortable apartment. What if I ended up with almost nothing? A fear like that can go unexamined, humming, shaping choices. Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius in the middle of a noisy Roman holiday, suggested an experiment. Not thinking about the fear. Trying it, on purpose, for a few days.
screen: `DAY THREE HUNDRED.` → `WHAT IF IT ALL WENT AWAY?` → `TRY IT ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: It's December in Rome, the festival of Saturnalia. The whole city is feasting; Seneca writes that Rome is sweating with it. In the middle of this he writes his eighteenth letter. His advice: set aside a certain number of days, and live on the scantiest, cheapest food, in rough, coarse clothing. And while you do, ask one question. In Richard Gummere's translation of 1917: "Is this the condition that I feared?" His reason is a picture everyone in Rome would know. Soldiers practice maneuvers in peacetime, digging trenches with no enemy in sight, so they won't panic when the real day comes. The soul should do the same in good times: train while fortune is kind, for the day fortune isn't. And it shouldn't be a show, like rich Romans who played at poverty in fancy little rooms. Make the bed really hard and the bread really coarse. A lovely detail: in the same letter Seneca quotes Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, who kept certain days of eating very little to see whether he was missing any real pleasure. Seneca borrows good ideas wherever he finds them, and says so. His bet is that the trial teaches something. The thing dreaded turns out to be survivable, even ordinary. Plain bread is still bread. A cold room is still a room. And a fear looked at in daylight has less room to hum. The point isn't to lose everything. It's to find out, ahead of time, what you'd still have.
screen: `SATURNALIA: ROME IS FEASTING.` · `LIVE ON VERY LITTLE FOR A FEW DAYS.` · `SOLDIERS DRILL IN PEACETIME.` · `SENECA QUOTES EPICURUS.` · then, large: `IS THIS WHAT I FEARED?`

segments.voice: Picture one small but real comfort, the second coffee, the phone at lunch, the car for a short trip, the soft chair, and imagine the moment you go without it. Let the little pang come. Then ask Seneca's question gently, and stay with whatever answer comes: is this what I feared?
Saturnalia, the Roman December feast when Seneca urged practicing poverty on purpose, so fear loses its grip in good times.
Your line: plain bread is still bread. Three hundred days, and i'm glad for every one of them.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners set aside occasional days of voluntary discomfort, like simple food or skipping a convenience, to see that what they fear losing is survivable.
